content: Entecavir is an antiviral medication used to treat chronic hepatitis B infection in both children and adults. Chronic hepatitis B is a significant global health issue, despite the availability of effective vaccines and antiviral therapies. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), in 2019, approximately 296 million people were living with chronic hepatitis B, with 1.5 million new infections occurring annually. Alarmingly, nearly 90% of infected individuals are unaware of their condition, and 78% of those diagnosed do not receive treatment. The prevalence of chronic hepatitis B varies by region, with the highest rates observed in the African region (8.83%) and the Western Pacific region (5.26%). Although China does not have the highest prevalence rate (5.49%), it accounts for one-third of the global chronic hepatitis B cases due to its large population. Chronic hepatitis B can manifest as either hepatitis B virus e antigen (HBeAg)-positive or HBeAg-negative. A 2006 study reported that 72% of chronic hepatitis B cases were HBeAg-negative, with higher proportions observed in individuals from Europe, the Middle East, and Africa. The virus is primarily transmitted through horizontal routes, such as injectable drug use, transfusion of infected blood, unhygienic tattooing practices, and unprotected sexual contact, as well as vertical transmission from mother to child. Mother-to-child transmission is particularly concerning, as it is a major cause of familial HBV infection. Without preventive measures, the risk of transmission from HBeAg-positive mothers is 70–90%, while for HBeAg-negative mothers, the risk is 10–40%. Approximately 90% of neonates and infants infected with HBV develop chronic hepatitis B, compared to only 5% of infected adults. Chronic hepatitis B significantly increases the risk of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma, which are leading causes of death in affected individuals. The primary goal of chronic hepatitis B treatment is to suppress HBV replication, reduce liver-related complications, and improve long-term survival. Antiviral therapies, including interferon-α (IFN-α) and nucleos(t)ide analogues, are the cornerstone of treatment. Entecavir, a nucleos(t)ide analogue, was approved for chronic hepatitis B treatment in 2005 in the United States and in 2006 in Europe. It has a high barrier to resistance, with a cumulative genotypic resistance rate of only 1.2% after six years in nucleos(t)ide-naïve individuals. However, resistance rates increase to 57% in individuals who are refractory to lamivudine. Entecavir and tenofovir have demonstrated similar effectiveness in achieving HBeAg clearance and seroconversion in nucleos(t)ide-naïve patients. Entecavir is generally well-tolerated, with most adverse reactions being mild to moderate. Serious adverse events occur in approximately 8% of patients, and the discontinuation rate due to adverse events is less than 1%. Additionally, entecavir is more cost-effective than other antiviral drugs, such as lamivudine and telbivudine, which is important for ensuring equitable access and long-term adherence to treatment. Entecavir is recommended as a first-line treatment for chronic hepatitis B in many clinical guidelines. It is approved for use in children aged two to 11 years, making it a preferred option for pediatric patients. In a randomized clinical trial, entecavir demonstrated significantly higher rates of HBeAg seroconversion and HBV DNA suppression compared to placebo after 48 weeks of treatment. Although lamivudine is also approved for children aged two years and older, it has a higher risk of resistance compared to entecavir. Entecavir works by inhibiting HBV reverse transcriptase through three mechanisms: base priming, reverse transcription of the negative strand DNA from pregenomic RNA, and synthesis of the positive strand of HBV DNA. It is phosphorylated to its active triphosphate form, with an intracellular half-life of 15 hours. In healthy individuals, peak plasma concentrations are reached within 0.5 to 1.5 hours, and steady-state levels are achieved after 6 to 10 days of once-daily dosing. The recommended dose for adults with chronic hepatitis B is 0.5 mg daily, but this increases to 1.0 mg daily for individuals with decompensated cirrhosis or lamivudine resistance. Long-term clinical studies have demonstrated the potent antiviral activity of entecavir, with HBV DNA response rates of approximately 95%. In a global multicenter study, 94% of HBeAg-positive patients achieved HBV DNA levels below 300 copies/mL, and 80% normalized their alanine aminotransferase (ALT) levels after five years of treatment. Another study in China showed that over 90% of nucleos(t)ide-naïve patients achieved undetectable HBV DNA levels after two years of entecavir therapy. Despite its widespread use and recommendation as a first-line treatment, the net effect of entecavir compared to no treatment or placebo has not been systematically reviewed. Randomized clinical trials have been conducted on this topic, but a comprehensive review is needed to evaluate the benefits and harms of entecavir in treating chronic hepatitis B. This review aims to address this gap in the literature and provide evidence-based recommendations for clinical practice.
